Assuredly
a-SHOOR-ed-lee
adv.
From assured, Old French asseurer, from Latin ad and securus, secure. Webster 1828: certainly; indubitably; without doubt. In Acts it introduces the conclusion of the first Christian sermon, and in Jeremiah it describes how God intends to plant His people.

Biblical Definition

Assuredly in Scripture marks a certainty that may be acted upon, and its greatest use closes the sermon at Pentecost: Therefore let all the house of Israel know assuredly, that God hath made that same Jesus, whom ye have crucified, both Lord and Christ (Acts 2:36). Peter does not ask for consideration; he demands certain knowledge of two facts joined in one sentence — that God has made Him Lord and Christ, and that this same Jesus is the one they crucified. Three thousand were pricked in their heart at it. Luke uses the word again of how Paul’s company read a vision: after he had seen the vision, immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia, assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us for to preach the gospel unto them (Acts 16:10) — a conclusion drawn, not a feeling followed. God uses it of His own settled purpose toward a restored people: I will rejoice over them to do them good, and I will plant them in this land assuredly with my whole heart and with my whole soul (Jeremiah 32:41). And Nathan puts it in Bathsheba’s mouth to hold David to an oath: Assuredly Solomon thy son shall reign after me, and he shall sit upon my throne (1 Kings 1:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ASSUREDLY as certainly; indubitably; without doubt or question; with entire confidence in the truth of what is affirmed.

expand to see more

ASSUREDLY, adv. — Certainly; indubitably; without doubt.

With full confidence or entire persuasion of the truth of a thing.

ASSURED, a. — Certain; indubitable; not doubting; bold to excess in some uses.

In theology, assurance is the settled persuasion of one’s own interest in Christ, grounded on the promises and the witness of the Spirit.

From Latin ad and securus, secure — the root also of sure, secure, and insurance.

Key Scripture

Acts 2:36 — "Therefore let all the house of Israel know assuredly, that God hath made that same Jesus, whom ye have crucified, both Lord and Christ."

Acts 16:10 — "And after he had seen the vision, immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia, assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us for to preach the gospel unto them."

Jeremiah 32:41 — "Yea, I will rejoice over them to do them good, and I will plant them in this land assuredly with my whole heart and with my whole soul."

1 Kings 1:13 — "Go and get thee in unto king David, and say unto him, Didst not thou, my lord, O king, swear unto thine handmaid, saying, Assuredly Solomon thy son shall reign after me, and he shall sit upon my throne? why then doth Adonijah reign?"

Modern Corruption

Acts 2:36 makes certain knowledge the aim of preaching, which the modern preference for tentative, exploratory religious language treats as arrogance rather than as the apostolic pattern.

expand to see more

Peter’s conclusion is the model, and every feature of it is now unfashionable. He addresses a specific audience — all the house of Israel. He demands certainty — know assuredly. He states a fact about a Person, publicly verifiable in its historical part. And he names his hearers’ own guilt without softening: whom ye have crucified. The response was not offence but conviction; they were pricked in their heart and asked what they should do. Preaching that offers perspectives, journeys, and invitations to explore has abandoned the form the apostles used. The dictionary does not confuse this certainty with the preacher’s self-confidence; the certainty is about Christ, and it is held by men who elsewhere describe themselves as the chief of sinners and as earthen vessels.

Jeremiah 32:41 shows the ground on which such certainty rests, and it is not the strength of anyone’s conviction. God says He will plant His people in the land assuredly with my whole heart and with my whole soul — an extraordinary anthropomorphism for the wholeheartedness of divine purpose, spoken to a prophet who had just bought a field in a country about to be destroyed. The chapter is the great biblical picture of faith acting on a promise against every visible fact: Jeremiah paid seventeen shekels for land under Babylonian occupation, weighed the money, signed the deed, and had it sealed in an earthen vessel that they may continue many days. Assurance of that kind is not a temperament; it is a conclusion drawn from what God has said.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek asphalos (G806), safely, certainly; sumbibazo (G4822), to knit together, to conclude; plerophoria (G4136), full assurance; Hebrew emeth (H571), truth, faithfulness.

expand to see more

Greek asphalos (G806) — safely, assuredly, beyond slipping; let all the house of Israel know assuredly (Acts 2:36).

Greek sumbibazo (G4822) — to knit together, and so to conclude by reasoning; assuredly gathering (Acts 16:10).

Greek plerophoria (G4136) — full assurance; the full assurance of understanding (Colossians 2:2) and of faith (Hebrews 10:22).

Hebrew emeth (H571) — truth, firmness, faithfulness; from aman, to be firm, the root of amen.

Hebrew omnam (H551) — verily, truly; the assuredly of 1 Kings 1:13.

Usage

"Let all the house of Israel know assuredly (Acts 2:36) — certain knowledge demanded, and three thousand pricked in heart."

"Assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us (Acts 16:10) — a conclusion drawn, not a feeling followed."

"I will plant them in this land assuredly with my whole heart (Jeremiah 32:41) — said to a man buying a field under occupation."
